lessons.intro: Many sequences grow by adding the same amount each time. Finding that amount, called the gap, is the fastest way to continue any pattern.

cards.b: Take each term away from the term after it. If every answer matches, that number is the gap and the rule is to add it.
Once you know the gap, add it to the last term to get the next one. Keep adding it to reach terms further along.
Check your gap on two or three known terms. If it works every time, your rule is right and you can answer with confidence.

fig.title: Adding 4 each time
fig.note: Each term is the one before plus 4.

ex.why: The gap is 3 because 5-2, 8-5 and 11-8 all equal 3. So the next term is 11+3, which is 14.

lessons.tip: Subtract two neighbouring terms first, because the gap usually shows itself at once.

quiz.why: The gap is 4, so 22+4 gives 26.
The gap is minus 3, so 21-3 gives 18.

lessons.t: Counting down by a fixed step
lessons.intro: Some sequences fall steadily rather than rise. Recognising a constant drop helps you spot patterns in countdowns, prices and falling scores.

cards.h: A falling gap is still a gap
cards.b: When terms get smaller, the gap is negative. Subtract the same amount at each step, or add a negative number.
Read the sequence from left to right and check whether each term is below the one before. Falling patterns often start high.
To jump several steps, multiply the gap by the number of steps and subtract the result. This avoids counting one step at a time.

fig.title: Each day drops by three
fig.note: Each bar is 3 shorter than the last.

ex.q: A tank holds 100 litres and loses 6 litres each hour. How much is left after 4 hours?
ex.why: Four hours at 6 litres is 24 litres lost. So 100-24 leaves 76 litres.

lessons.tip: Multiply the gap by the number of steps to skip ahead quickly.

quiz.why: The gap is minus 5, so 35-5 gives 30.
The gap is minus 6, so 54-6 gives 48.

lessons.intro: Not every sequence adds a fixed amount. Some multiply by the same number each time, and doubling is the most common example you will meet.

cards.b: Divide each term by the one before it. If the answer is the same every time, the sequence multiplies by that number rather than adding.
Each term is twice the one before, so the numbers climb quickly. Ten doublings from 1 reach 1024.
Check the ratio on two pairs of terms. A rule that works once is not enough, so confirm it on at least one more pair.

fig.title: Finding a doubling rule
fig.note: Same ratio each time means multiply.

ex.why: Each term is double the one before, so 24 times 2 gives 48.

lessons.tip: If the numbers climb faster and faster, look for a multiplier instead of a gap.

quiz.why: Each term doubles, so 40 times 2 gives 80.
Each term doubles, so 56 times 2 gives 112.

lessons.intro: The same idea works for any fixed multiplier, such as three, four or ten. Once you can spot a ratio, you can continue almost any multiplying sequence.

cards.b: A sequence may multiply by 3, 4 or 10 each time. The method is the same: divide a term by the one before it to find the ratio.
To find an earlier term, divide the known term by the multiplier. This reverses the pattern one step at a time.
A ratio of one half means the terms shrink. Halving 80 gives 40, then 20, so each term is half the one before.

fig.title: Each term times three
fig.note: The ratio between terms is 3.

ex.why: Each term is three times the one before, and 108 times 3 is 324.

lessons.tip: Test a suspected multiplier on the second pair as well as the first.

quiz.why: Each term is ten times the last, so 1000 times 10 gives 10000.
Each term halves the one before, so 12 divided by 2 gives 6.

lessons.t: Filling a gap in the middle
lessons.intro: Puzzles often hide one term in the middle of a sequence. You can find it by using the terms on either side, which share the same rule.

cards.b: A missing term sits between two known terms. Compare the known term before it with the one after it to see the total change.
If the sequence goes from 4 to 16 across three steps, the total change is 12 and each step is 4. Divide the total change by the number of steps to find the rule.
Put your answer back in and confirm both sides still work. A correct filling keeps every gap equal.

fig.title: Filling a hidden term
fig.note: Use the neighbours to set the rule.

ex.why: The gap is 4, since 8+4 is 12 and 12+4 is 16. So the missing term is 12.

lessons.tip: Divide the total change between two known terms by the steps between them.

quiz.why: The gap is 4, so 3+4 gives 7 and 7+4 gives 11.
The gap is minus 8, so 52-8 gives 44 and 44-8 gives 36.

lessons.intro: Bigger gaps, such as 9 or 25, work exactly like small ones. The key is to subtract carefully and avoid arithmetic slips that spoil the rule.

cards.b: A gap of 25 is no harder than a gap of 2. Subtract one term from the next to find it, and check the subtraction twice.
Subtracting 48 from 57 gives 9, but two-digit numbers are easy to slip on. Write the sum out in columns when in doubt.
Round the gap to a nearby number to see whether your answer is sensible. If the terms rise by about 10, a result of 40 is too large.

fig.title: Gap of nine each time
fig.note: Each term is 9 more than the last.

ex.why: The gap is 9, so 75 plus 9 gives 84.

lessons.tip: Round the gap to a friendly number to check your answer.

quiz.why: The gap is 15, so 165 plus 15 gives 180.
The gap is 25, so 275 plus 25 gives 300.

lessons.intro: Sequences can pass below zero, and the gap still applies. Knowing how to step past zero keeps your pattern reading accurate in harder puzzles.

cards.b: On a number line, -3 sits below 0 and -1 sits above -3. A sequence that falls by 5 each time moves left past zero.
A gap of minus 5 means you subtract 5. So 4 minus 5 gives -1, and -1 minus 5 gives -6.
When a sequence crosses zero, count the steps in order rather than guessing. Each step still changes the value by the same gap.

fig.title: Stepping past zero
fig.note: Negative gaps move the value left.

ex.why: The gap is minus 5, so -6 minus 5 gives -11.

lessons.tip: Read a negative gap as subtract this amount, and the signs stay simple.

quiz.why: Each step subtracts 3, so -6 minus 3 gives -9.
The gap is plus 3, so -1 plus 3 gives 2.

lessons.intro: Gaps are not always whole numbers. Sequences in measurements and money often step by halves or decimals, so you need to read those gaps just as carefully.

cards.b: Subtract 1.5 from 2.0 to get 0.5. Line up the decimal points so each digit lands in the right column.
A gap of one half means every two steps add a whole number. Counting halves in a row helps you spot the rhythm.
A bus fare that rises by 25p each year is a sequence with a gap of 0.25 pounds. Adding that gap each year gives the next fare.

fig.title: Steps of half a unit
fig.note: Each term is 0.5 more than the last.

ex.why: The gap is 0.5, so 1.9 plus 0.5 gives 2.4.

lessons.tip: Write decimals with the same number of places before you subtract.

quiz.why: The gap is 0.5, so 3.6 plus 0.5 gives 4.1.
The gap is minus 0.75, so 7.75 minus 0.75 gives 7.

lessons.t: Working backwards from a known term
lessons.intro: Sometimes a puzzle gives you a later term and asks for an earlier one. Reversing the rule lets you find the start of a sequence from any point in it.

cards.b: If each step adds 6, the term before any term is that term minus 6. Use the opposite operation to move back.
If each term is three times the last, divide a term by 3 to find the one before it. Check your answer by multiplying back up.
Once you know the rule and one term, write out a few terms to confirm they match the clues. This catches mistakes early.

fig.title: Working back from 13
fig.note: Each term is 6 more than the one before.

ex.q: A sequence goes up by 6 each time, and 13 is followed by 19. What term came before 13?
ex.why: Reverse the gap by subtracting 6 from 13, which gives 7. Check that 7 plus 6 equals 13.

lessons.tip: Use the opposite operation, such as dividing for multiplying, when moving back.

quiz.q: A sequence doubles each time, and 40 is the term that follows some earlier number. What is that earlier number?
quiz.why: Dividing 40 by 2 reverses the doubling and gives 20.

quiz.q: Each term is 7 more than the one before it. What term came before 50?
quiz.why: Subtracting 7 from 50 gives 43.

lessons.intro: Two sequences can look alike at first, yet one adds and the other multiplies. Checking the gap and the ratio side by side shows which rule is at work.

cards.b: Subtract neighbouring terms. If the differences are equal, the rule adds; if the differences grow, the rule probably multiplies.
Divide neighbouring terms. If the ratio stays the same, the rule multiplies, so check the ratios as well as the gaps.

cards.h: Test the rule on every pair
cards.b: A rule must work for every pair in the sequence. Test the last pair too, so a rule that only fits the start is rejected.

fig.title: Adding or multiplying?
fig.note: Check gaps first, then ratios.

ex.why: Each term is double the last, since 6 times 2 is 12, while adding 3 would give 9.

lessons.tip: Equal gaps point to adding, while gaps that grow point to multiplying.

quiz.why: Each term is 5 more than the one before, so the rule adds 5.
Each term doubles, since 8 times 2 is 16, while multiplying by 4 would give 64.

lessons.t: Checking a rule across the whole sequence
lessons.intro: A rule that works for the first two terms can still fail later. Checking every pair is the final step that turns a guess into a confident answer.

cards.b: Write down the gap or ratio for each neighbouring pair. A genuine rule gives the same answer for every pair in the sequence.

cards.h: Watch for a change of rule
cards.b: Sometimes the gap changes partway through. If the differences are 2, 2, 2 and then 5, the sequence does not follow one simple gap.
Describe the rule in one sentence, such as add 4 each time. A clear sentence makes it easy to spot a mistake.

fig.title: Checking a rule thoroughly
fig.note: Only accept a rule that fits all pairs.

ex.why: The gaps are 1, 2, 3, 4, rising by one each time, while a fixed gap or doubling fails at the second pair.

lessons.tip: Test your rule on the last pair, not only the first.

quiz.why: The gaps are 3, 4, 5, 6, so a fixed gap fails at the second pair.
The gap switches between minus 2 and plus 2, so subtracting 2 each time fails at the second pair.

lessons.intro: Some sequences do not use one rule. They alternate between two steps, so you must check which step comes next before you add anything.

cards.b: Compare terms two places apart to see the pattern in each half. If the odd positions and even positions each follow their own gap, the rule alternates.
Write the two steps as a pair, such as plus 3 then minus 4. Repeat the pair until you reach the missing term.
Count how many terms you have passed so you know which step to use next. Losing track is the most common error in these puzzles.

fig.title: Plus three, minus four
fig.note: The steps alternate: +3, -4, +3, -4.

ex.why: The steps alternate, plus 3 then minus 4. The last step was minus 4, so the next is plus 3, giving 11.

lessons.tip: Write the two steps on paper so the alternation is obvious.

quiz.why: The steps alternate between plus 3 and minus 4, so 4 plus 3 gives 7.
The steps alternate between minus 5 and plus 3, so 16 minus 5 gives 11.

lessons.intro: A pattern can repeat a short block of steps over and over. Once you spot the block, you can predict every later term without counting from the start.

cards.b: Look for a set of steps that repeats, such as plus 2 then plus 1. Group the steps into a block to see the whole pattern.
Each new block starts where the last one ended. Add the block's steps in order to get the next few terms.

cards.h: Use the block to skip ahead
cards.b: To find a far term, count how many full blocks fit before it. This is faster than writing out every term.

fig.title: A block of two steps
fig.note: The two steps keep repeating.

ex.why: The steps repeat as plus 2 then plus 1, and the last step was plus 1, so 9 plus 2 gives 11.

lessons.tip: Name the block in two or three words so you remember it.

quiz.why: The block is plus 3 then plus 1, so the next step after 9 is plus 3, giving 12.
The block is minus 2 then plus 1, so 8 minus 2 gives 6.

lessons.intro: Sometimes the gap itself changes in a simple way. When each gap is one larger than the last, you can predict the next term by extending the list of gaps.

cards.b: Subtract each pair of neighbours and list the gaps in order. Growing gaps usually follow a simple counting pattern.
If the gaps are 1, 2, 3, the next gap is 4. Add that gap to the last term to get the next term in the sequence.
A rule that adds one more each time is a growing gap rule. It is different from a constant gap rule, so check the gaps carefully.

fig.title: Gaps of 1, 2, 3, 4
fig.note: Each gap is one more than the last.

ex.why: The gaps are 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5 and 13 plus 5 gives 18.

lessons.tip: Write the gap list first, since the pattern usually shows up there.

quiz.why: The gaps are 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5 and 12 plus 5 gives 17.
The gaps grow 1, 2, 3, 4, so the next gap is 5 and 20 plus 5 gives 25.

lessons.intro: Gaps can also grow in bigger steps. Spotting a growth of two each time lets you predict how quickly the sequence will accelerate.

cards.b: Compare each gap with the one before it to see how much it grows. If the gaps go up by 2 each time, the growth step is 2.
Begin with the first gap and add the growth step to find the next gap. Then add each gap to the sequence in turn.
Growing gaps make a sequence accelerate, so the terms climb faster and faster. Expect large numbers later in the list.

fig.title: Gaps grow by two
fig.note: Each gap is 2 bigger than the last.

ex.why: The gaps are 2, 4, 6, 8, so the next gap is 10 and 21 plus 10 gives 31.

lessons.tip: Write the gaps underneath the terms so the growth is visible.

quiz.why: The gaps are 2, 4, 6, 8, so the next gap is 10 and 20 plus 10 gives 30.
The gaps are 3, 5, 7, 9, so the next gap is 11 and 28 plus 11 gives 39.

lessons.intro: Square numbers, such as 1, 4, 9 and 16, come from gaps that go up by two each time. Recognising them helps you spot numbers that arise from grids and areas.

cards.b: A square number is a whole number times itself, such as 4 times 4 giving 16. Start with 1 times 1 and build up from there.
The gaps are 3, 5, 7 and 9 between 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. Each gap is the next odd number after the one before.
A square tile grid with 5 tiles along each side has 25 tiles. Picturing the grid helps you remember the square pattern.

fig.title: Square numbers in a table
fig.note: Each cell is a whole number squared.

ex.why: These are the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25, so the next is 6 times 6, which is 36.

lessons.tip: Learn the squares up to 12 by heart, since they save time in many puzzles.

quiz.why: These are square numbers, so the next one is 7 times 7, which is 49.

quiz.q: What is the gap between the square numbers 36 and 49?
quiz.why: The gap is 49 minus 36, which is 13.

lessons.intro: Triangular numbers count the dots in a stacked triangle. Their gaps grow by one each time, which makes them a good test of your growing-gap skills.

cards.h: Build the triangle row by row
cards.b: The first triangle has 1 dot, the next has 3 and the next has 6. Each row adds one more dot than the row above.
The gaps between 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15 are 2, 3, 4 and 5. Each gap equals the number of dots in the new row.
A triangle of 4 rows has 1+2+3+4 dots, which is 10. Adding the row sizes gives the same numbers as the sequence.

fig.title: Building triangle numbers
fig.note: Each new row adds one more dot.

ex.why: The gaps are 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next gap is 6 and 15 plus 6 gives 21.

lessons.tip: Triangular numbers are sums of counting numbers, so 1+2+3 gives 6.

quiz.q: What comes after 21 in the triangular numbers?
quiz.why: The next gap is 7, and 21 plus 7 gives 28.

quiz.q: How many dots are in a triangle with 5 rows?
quiz.why: Adding 1+2+3+4+5 gives 15.

lessons.intro: Some rules combine two steps in one: double the last term, then add one. Breaking the rule into those two parts makes it easy to check each term.

cards.b: Read the rule as double, then add one. Treat each part separately and you will avoid many arithmetic slips.
Apply the double-and-add rule to one known term to confirm it gives the next. Then repeat the check on a second pair.
Each term here is one less than a power of two, such as 3, 7, 15 and 31. Spotting this shortcut can help with large terms.

fig.title: Double, then add one
fig.note: Each term is double the last plus 1.

ex.why: Double 31 to get 62, then add 1 to get 63.

lessons.tip: Double first, then add one, so the order of operations stays clear.

quiz.why: Each term is double the last plus 1, so 23 doubled is 46 and adding 1 gives 47.
Each term is double the last plus 1, so 7 doubled plus 1 gives 15.

lessons.intro: Mixing addition and multiplication in one sequence can look confusing. Taking the steps one at a time, in a fixed order, keeps the pattern clear.

cards.b: Write down whether each step adds or multiplies, then group the steps in pairs. The pair repeats, so the pattern becomes predictable.
Apply the steps in sequence and never skip one. Multiplying before you add gives a different answer, so keep to the order.
Terms in odd and even places often follow different steps. Look at positions one, three and five separately to check.

fig.title: Two steps repeat
fig.note: Add 2, then multiply by 2.

ex.why: The steps alternate between add 2 and multiply by 2, so 20 plus 2 gives 22.

lessons.tip: Label each step as add or multiply before you calculate.

quiz.why: The steps alternate between add 2 and multiply by 2, so 32 plus 2 gives 34.
The steps alternate between multiply by 2 and minus 5, so 14 minus 5 gives 9.

lessons.t: Alternating signs as well as sizes
lessons.intro: Some sequences change both their size and their sign at every step. Splitting the pattern into a size rule and a sign rule makes the next term easy to find.

cards.b: Ignore the minus signs at first and look at the sizes alone. Then add the signs back in, which alternate in this kind of sequence.
The first term tells you where the signs start, so confirm whether it is positive or negative. Getting the start wrong flips the whole answer.
Multiply the size by the sign to get each term. This method works for any sequence built from a size rule and a sign rule.

fig.title: Two rules, one sequence
fig.note: Combine the size and the sign.

ex.why: The sizes go up by 2 each time, and the signs alternate, so the fifth term is plus 10.

lessons.tip: Write the sign above each term to see the alternation at a glance.

quiz.why: The sizes count up by 1 and the sign alternates, so the fifth term is plus 5.
The sizes go up by 5 each time and the sign alternates, so the next term is minus 25.

lessons.t: Spotting the term that breaks a rule
lessons.intro: Puzzles sometimes include one term that does not follow the rest. Finding it quickly means checking the gap at each step, not just the first few.

cards.b: Work out each gap in turn and look for the one that is different. The odd gap is usually where the mistake sits.
Once you know the rule, calculate what the term should be. Compare that value with the one given in the list.

cards.h: Do not change the whole rule
cards.b: A single wrong term is usually a typo or a trap, not a new rule. Keep the rule that fits most terms and fix the one that does not.

fig.title: Right rule or broken term?
fig.note: Find the term whose gap is off.

ex.q: Which term breaks the pattern in 3, 6, 9, 12, 16, 18?
ex.why: The gap is 3, so the fifth term should be 15, and 16 is the term that breaks the pattern.

lessons.tip: Check the gap on either side of any term that looks suspicious.

quiz.q: Which term breaks the pattern in 5, 10, 15, 21, 25?
quiz.why: The gap is 5, so the fourth term should be 20, and 21 breaks the pattern.

quiz.q: Which term breaks the pattern in 100, 90, 80, 71, 60?
quiz.why: The gap is minus 10, so the fourth term should be 70, and 71 is the broken term.

lessons.intro: Some sequences zig-zag while their gaps grow, so each step goes up and then down by a larger amount. Tracking both size and direction is the key skill.

cards.b: Write each gap with its sign, such as +1, -2, +3. The size grows by one each step and the sign alternates.
Treat the sign and the size as two separate rules. Work out each one, then combine them to get the next term.
Once the rule is clear, you can jump several terms by adding the next few signed gaps. Check at least two terms to be sure.

fig.title: Up one, down two, up three

ex.why: The gaps are +1, -2, +3, -4, so the next gap is +5 and 0 plus 5 gives 5.

lessons.tip: Write the signs in a column, and the alternation jumps out.

quiz.why: The gaps are +1, -2, +3, -4, so the next gap is +5 and 8 plus 5 gives 13.
The gaps are -1, +2, -3, +4, so the next gap is -5 and 2 minus 5 gives -3.

lessons.t: Reading a grid across its rows
lessons.intro: A grid is a rectangle of numbers with a rule running across each row. Reading that rule row by row is the first step to filling any missing cell.

cards.h: Read each row left to right
cards.b: Look at how one row changes from left to right. In this grid each row adds 1 to reach the next cell.
Once you know the row rule, check where each row starts. Here each row begins three more than the row above.
Use the row rule to find the missing cell in its row. Then check its column to confirm your answer.

fig.title: Each row counts up by one
fig.note: Rows step by one, and each row starts three higher.

ex.q: A grid has rows 2, 4, 6 then 5, 7, 9 then 8, 10, ?. What belongs in the empty cell?
ex.why: Each row goes up by 2, so 10 plus 2 gives 12, and the row starts rise by 3 as 2, 5, 8 shows.

lessons.tip: Read the first two cells of a row, then test the rule on the third.

quiz.q: Row one is 3, 6, 9 and row two is 4, 7, ?. What is the missing cell?
quiz.why: Row two also goes up by 3, so 7 plus 3 gives 10.

quiz.q: Row one is 2, 4, 6, 8 and row two is 3, 5, 7, ?. What is the missing cell?
quiz.why: Row two goes up by 2, so 7 plus 2 gives 9.

lessons.t: Reading a grid down its columns
lessons.intro: The same grid can also be read down each column. Checking columns gives you a second route to the answer and catches errors that row reading misses.

cards.b: Look from the top to the bottom of a column to find its rule. In this grid each column rises by two going down.
A good grid rule works across and down. If your row rule and column rule disagree, you have made a mistake.
Pick whichever direction has more clues. Filled columns often make the missing value easier to find.

fig.title: Columns rise by two
fig.note: Each column goes up by 2 going down.

ex.q: Column one reads 1, 3, 5 going down, and column two reads 2, 4, ? going down. What is the missing value?
ex.why: Column two rises by 2 going down, so 4 plus 2 gives 6.

lessons.tip: Trace one column with your finger before deciding the rule.

quiz.q: A column reads 9, 7, 5 from top to bottom. What comes next?
quiz.why: The column falls by 2 each time, so 5 minus 2 gives 3.

quiz.q: A column reads 10, 20, 30, ?. What comes next?
quiz.why: The column rises by 10 each time, so 30 plus 10 gives 40.

lessons.t: Each column adds to the same total
lessons.intro: Some grids follow a total rule rather than a step rule. When every column adds up to the same number, the missing cell is whatever makes its column total correct.

cards.b: A grid may be built so that every column adds to the same number. Find that total using a complete column first.
For an incomplete column, add the filled cells and subtract that sum from the target total. The difference is the missing value.
Confirm the total works for each column. A correct grid passes every check.

fig.title: Each column totals 15
fig.note: The missing cell in column three is 6.

ex.q: Each column totals 12. A column reads 5, 4, ? so what is missing?
ex.why: The column needs 12, and 5 plus 4 gives 9, so the missing cell is 12 minus 9, which is 3.

lessons.tip: Find the total from a complete column before filling any gap.

quiz.q: Each row of a grid totals 10. A row reads 2, 5, ?. What is the missing number?
quiz.why: The row needs 10, and 2 plus 5 gives 7, so 10 minus 7 gives 3.

quiz.q: Each column totals 20. A column reads 6, 7, 4 and one blank. What fills the blank?
quiz.why: The filled cells sum to 17, and 20 minus 17 gives 3.

lessons.intro: A multiplication table is a grid where each cell is its row number times its column number. Once you see this, many grid puzzles become simple.

cards.b: Each cell equals its row label times its column label. Row 2 and column 3 give 2 times 3, which is 6.
The table mirrors itself across the diagonal, so row 3, column 2 must match row 2, column 3. This doubles your checks.
If a cell is blank, work out the two labels that meet there. Multiply them and write the product in the gap.

fig.title: Products in a small table
fig.note: Each cell is its row times its column.

ex.q: In a multiplication grid, row 4 and column 6 meet at what number?
ex.why: Multiply the row label 4 by the column label 6 to get 24.

lessons.tip: Start with the easy products like 1 times and 10 times, then build the rest.

quiz.q: In a multiplication grid, the cell where row 7 meets column 3 holds what?
quiz.why: Seven times 3 is 21.

quiz.q: What value sits where row 5 meets column 5 in a multiplication grid?
quiz.why: Five times 5 is 25.

lessons.intro: Some grids double across each row and down each column. Checking the rule in both directions tells you the multiplier and confirms the missing cell.

cards.b: Divide each cell by the one before it in its row. A ratio of 2 across each row means the rule doubles.
Repeat the check down the columns. The same ratio in both directions is strong evidence that you have the right rule.
The bottom-right cell follows from the row or column rule. Multiply the cell before it by the ratio to get 16 here.

fig.title: Doubling both ways
fig.note: Each cell is double the one before it.

ex.q: A row doubles at each step and reads 5, 10, 20, ?. What is the next cell?
ex.why: Each cell doubles the one before, so 20 times 2 gives 40.

lessons.tip: Test the ratio on two neighbours before assuming it holds across the grid.

quiz.q: A column doubles at each step: 6, 12, 24, ?. What is the next cell?
quiz.why: Each step doubles, so 24 times 2 gives 48.

quiz.q: A row goes 1, 3, 9, ?, where each cell triples the one before. What is the next cell?
quiz.why: Each cell is three times the last, so 9 times 3 gives 27.

lessons.t: Shapes that move across a grid
lessons.intro: Grids can hold shapes instead of numbers. Each shape appears once in every row and every column, so you can find the gap by elimination.

cards.b: In this kind of grid, each shape appears once in every row and every column. Count the shapes already placed to see which one is missing.
Cross off any shape already in the row or column of the gap. The one left over is the answer.
Confirm the missing shape also fits its column. A correct answer completes the row and column with three different shapes.

fig.title: One of each per line
fig.note: Every row and column holds all three shapes.

ex.q: A row already holds a circle and a square. Which shape fills the last cell?
ex.why: The row already has a circle and a square, so the third shape must be the triangle.

lessons.tip: Scan both the row and the column of the gap, not just one line.

quiz.q: A column holds a circle and a triangle above a blank, in a grid of three shapes. Which shape goes in the blank?
quiz.why: The column already has a circle and a triangle, so the blank must be the square.

quiz.q: In a row of three shapes, a square and a circle are already placed. Which shape is left?
quiz.why: Only the triangle remains once the square and circle are placed.

lessons.t: Counting in two directions at once
lessons.intro: Grids often change by one amount across and by another amount down. Finding both amounts lets you fill any cell without counting from the corner.

cards.b: Find the step across each row and the step down each column. In this grid the step across is 2 and the step down is 1.
Use the top-left cell as the start. Add the down step to move down and the across step to move across.
Reaching a cell by moving across and by moving down must give the same answer. If not, recheck your steps.

fig.title: Two steps, two directions
fig.note: Across adds 2 and down adds 1 here.

ex.q: Row one of a grid is 10, 20, 30 and column one reads 10, 11, 12 going down. What is in row two, column two?
ex.why: Row two goes 11, 21, 31 since each row adds 10, so the cell in column two is 21.

lessons.tip: Find the two steps first, and the rest of the grid is just addition.

quiz.q: Across each step adds 3 and down each step adds 2. The top-left cell is 1. What is row two, column two?
quiz.why: Going down adds 2 to give 3, then going across adds 3 to give 6.

quiz.q: Using the same grid, what is row one, column three?
quiz.why: Across the top row, the values are 1, 4, 7.

lessons.intro: Some grids follow a rule along the diagonal from corner to corner. Spotting the diagonal pattern can give you a faster route to the missing cell.

cards.b: Follow the cells from top-left to bottom-right. Their values often rise by a fixed amount along that line.
Each cell next to the diagonal is one more than its neighbour. Use this to check that your diagonal rule matches the rest of the grid.
Continue the diagonal rule to reach the missing corner. Then confirm the cell fits its row and its column.

fig.title: Diagonal steps up by two
fig.note: Diagonal cells: 1, 3, 5.

ex.q: Diagonal cells of a grid read 2, 5, 8, ?. What is the next diagonal cell?
ex.why: The diagonal steps by 3, so 8 plus 3 gives 11.

lessons.tip: Highlight the diagonal in pencil so the pattern stands out.

quiz.q: Diagonal cells of a grid read 4, 7, 10, ?. What comes next?
quiz.why: The diagonal steps by 3, so 10 plus 3 gives 13.

quiz.q: Diagonal cells read 1, 4, 9, 16, ?. What comes next?
quiz.why: These are square numbers, so the next is 5 times 5, which is 25.

lessons.t: Squares that shift along a grid
lessons.intro: A grid can repeat the same numbers, shifted one place in each row. Here the squares slide along, so each row is built from the one above it.

cards.b: Compare each row with the row above. Here each row is the one above shifted one place to the left, with a new square added at the end.
The values are square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25. Each one is the square of its position along the diagonal.
The cells on the diagonal from top-left are 1, 9 and 25, which are odd square numbers. Each one is the next odd square after the one before.

fig.title: Shifting squares along rows
fig.note: Each row is the row above shifted left.

ex.q: Row three reads 9, 16, ?. What is the missing cell?
ex.why: Row three is row two shifted left, so the new square after 16 is 25.

lessons.tip: Know the squares up to 12 by heart, since they save time in grid puzzles.

quiz.q: A row reads 1, 4, 9, 16. Which square comes next?
quiz.why: The next square after 16 is 5 times 5, which is 25.
Seven times 7 is 49.

lessons.t: Testing a guess against the grid
lessons.intro: A guess can look right in one row and still fail elsewhere. Testing your candidate against every row and column is the surest way to finish a grid.

cards.b: Suggest a value for the blank from the nearest clue. Write it down so you can test it against the rest of the grid.
Check that the guess fits the pattern in its row and its column. A value that fits only one line is not yet proven.
If one check fails, try the next candidate. Narrow the options with the rule rather than guessing at random.

fig.title: Testing a guess
fig.note: Only keep a guess that passes both checks.

ex.q: A row doubles at each step and reads 5, 10, ?. Your first guess is 15. Does it pass?
ex.why: Doubling 10 gives 20, not 15, so the guess fails the row check and must be rejected.

lessons.tip: Test your guess against the rule before you write it in.

quiz.q: A column reads 2, 4, ? going down, with a step of 2. What fits?
quiz.why: The column adds 2 each step, so 4 plus 2 gives 6.

quiz.q: A row reads 3, 7, 11, then a blank. Your guess is 15. Does it pass the row check?
quiz.why: The row adds 4 each step, so 11 plus 4 gives 15, and the guess passes.

lessons.intro: Bigger grids follow the same method, just with more cells. Find the step across and the step down, then fill the corner.

cards.b: A bigger grid still uses a row step and a column step. Measure both from the cells you can see before filling anything.
Look at the first number of each row to find the step down. The starts here go 1, 5, 9 and 13, a jump of 4 each time.
The last cell is the start of its row plus three steps across. Here 13 plus 3 gives 16.

fig.title: Four columns, four rows
fig.note: Across adds 1; down adds 4.

ex.q: Row starts in a grid go 2, 7, 12. Each row goes up by 1 across, and each row has four cells. What is the last cell of row three?
ex.why: Row three starts at 12 and goes up 1 each cell, so the fourth cell is 15.

lessons.tip: Read the first column before the grid gets crowded, to find the step down.

quiz.q: Row starts go 1, 3, 5 down a grid, and each row goes up 2 across. What is row three's second cell?
quiz.why: Row three starts at 5 and adds 2, so its second cell is 7.

quiz.q: Row starts go 4, 8, 12, 16, and each row goes up by 1 across. What is row four's third cell?
quiz.why: Row four starts at 16, so its third cell is 16 plus 2, which is 18.

lessons.t: Finding the rule from the whole grid
lessons.intro: The final skill is to combine every clue: row steps, column steps and any starting values. Checking the whole grid tells you which cells are correct before you finish.

cards.b: List the row steps and column steps before you fill anything. Two clues usually give you the rule for the whole grid.
Find the blank once from its row and once from its column. If both routes give the same value, the answer is secure.

cards.h: State the rule in one line
cards.b: Say the rule in a sentence, such as add 10 across and 5 down. A clear rule makes it easy to spot any mistake.

fig.title: Across 10, down 5
fig.note: Across adds 10; down adds 5.

ex.q: A grid has row steps of 3 across and column steps of 2 down, starting at 1 in the top-left. What is the value in row three, column three?
ex.why: Going down two rows adds 4 to 1, giving 5, and going across two columns adds 6, giving 11.

lessons.tip: When two routes give the same answer, you can trust it.

quiz.q: A grid adds 10 across and 5 down, and the top-left cell is 10. What is row two, column one?
quiz.why: Going down one row adds 5 to 10, giving 15.

quiz.q: Using the same grid with top-left 10, what is row one, column four?
quiz.why: Across three columns add 10 each, so 10 plus 30 gives 40.
